topic.name: Singular Value Decomposition of 2x2 Matrices With Zero or Repeated Eigenvalues

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 2\sqrt{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $\Sigma,$ we can deduce that $\sigma_1=2\sqrt{5}$ and $\sigma_2=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=20,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 20 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10 \end{bmatrix} - 20 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & -10 \\ -10 & -10 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 20I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & -10 \\ -10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 0I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A A^T$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows: \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{2} \\ -3\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \] such that \[ \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1. \]

    Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} x_1 - \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} x_2 = 0, \] we get a nonzero solution $\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the second column of $U\mathbin{:}$ \[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt2 & 1 \\ 2 & \sqrt2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt2 & 1 \\ 2 & \sqrt2 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt2 & 1 \\ 2 & \sqrt2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt2 & 2 \\ 1 & \sqrt2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt2 & 1 \\ 2 & \sqrt2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3\sqrt2 \\ 3\sqrt2 &3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $\Sigma,$ we can deduce that $\sigma_1=3$ and $\sigma_2=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=9,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 9 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3\sqrt2 \\ 3\sqrt2 &3 \end{bmatrix} - 9 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 3\sqrt2 \\ 3\sqrt2 &-6 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 9I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3\sqrt2 \\ 3\sqrt2 &3 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3\sqrt2 \\ 3\sqrt2 &3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 0I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A A^T$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows: \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt2 & 1 \\ 2 & \sqrt2\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt3} \\ 3\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \] such that \[ \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1. \]

    Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} x_1+ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} x_2 = 0, \] we get a nonzero solution $\begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the second column of $U\mathbin{:}$ \[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} & -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices $A$ and $\Sigma$ shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $\Sigma,$ we can deduce that $\sigma_1= \sqrt{2}$ and $\sigma_2=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$):

    • For $\lambda_1=\sigma_1^2=2,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 2 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 2I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

    • For $\lambda_2=\sigma_2^2=0,$ we have \begin{align*} A^T \! A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A^T \! A - 0I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ gives a unit eigenvector
      \[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A A^T$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows: \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    Since the second singular value is $\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \] such that \[ \mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \|\mathbf{u}_2\|=1. \]

    Solving $\mathbf{u}_1 \cdot \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ which is equivalent to \[ - x_1 +0x_2 = 0, \] we get the solution \[ \mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} -1 &0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix With a Zero Eigenvalue

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 1& -\sqrt5\\ \sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrix shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1& -\sqrt5\\ \sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1& -\sqrt5\\ \sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1& \sqrt5\\ -\sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1& -\sqrt5\\ \sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: Notice that since $A^T \! A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are

    $\qquad$ $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sqrt{6}.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$): Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T\!A-6I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0},$ we obtain the unit eigenvectors

    $\qquad$ $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

    • First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} 1& -\sqrt5\\ \sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    • Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} 1& -\sqrt5\\ \sqrt5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ \sqrt5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \sqrt{ \dfrac{5}{6}} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt{ \dfrac{5}{6}}& \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} &\sqrt{ \dfrac{5}{6}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{6} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{6} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \]

example.title: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

question.text: \[ A =\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrix shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
question.explanation:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute $A^T \! A\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} A^T \! A &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: Notice that since $A^T \! A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are

    $\qquad$ $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1.$

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \! A$): Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T\!A-1I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0},$ we obtain the unit eigenvectors

    $\qquad$ $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

    • First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_1} A\mathbf{v}_1 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

    • Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{\sigma_2} A\mathbf{v}_2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \end{align*}

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\Sigma,$ and $V\mathbin{:}$

\[ U = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
